notes:
I've written notes for most verses, but there are real gaps. My search tool hit its usage limit partway through, so I couldn't search for the Catholic, Orthodox, modern-scholarship or prosperity-teaching views, or for each Protestant tradition's own teachers. Section 3 is missing, and section 2 has only the few disagreements that showed up in the commentary pages I had already read. Verse 14 has only one point and verse 16 has very little.

Some points come from collected-commentary pages (biblehub.com/commentaries/1_timothy/6-x.htm) where my copy of the page didn't show who wrote each entry. I name a commentator only where the page did, and otherwise say "an entry on the page."

## 1. Traditional reading, verse by verse

**v. 1**
- Ellicott: Paul turns from church officers to Christian slaves, which he calls perhaps the hardest question the early church faced. Here he means slaves of pagan masters. They must not think the faith will make master and slave equal on earth. If they became sullen or rebellious, outsiders would blame God and the gospel. Ellicott adds that slavery has since been disappearing from the world. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_timothy/6.htm
- Calvin: People naturally resent being ruled. Slaves should not ask whether they deserve a better lot, and should truly respect their masters, because authority comes from God even when the person holding it is unworthy. Some slaves argued that people who serve the devil shouldn't rule God's children. Paul turns this around: they should obey so the gospel isn't accused of breeding rebellion. https://ccel.org/wwsb/1Timothy/6 and https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cal/1-timothy-6.html
- Gill: "Yoke" here means being under human masters (bought, hired or apprenticed), not the yoke of God's law or of Christ. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-timothy/6-1.html
- Barnes: Christianity taught patient endurance of wrongs, slavery included. This verse is mainly about masters who were not Christians. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bnb/1-timothy-6.html and https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-timothy/6-1.html
- Coffman: New freedom in Christ might tempt slaves to look down on their masters. Christianity makes anyone a better worker. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-timothy/6-1.html
- Preacher's Homiletical Commentary: Pagan masters would come to respect a faith that made their slaves honest and hard-working, and many were won that way. It says Christianity ended slavery by planting principles, not by stirring up political anger. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/phc/1-timothy-6.html
- Guzik: Poor or disrespectful work makes people judge Christianity false. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-timothy-6/

**v. 2**
- Guzik: Slaves of Christian masters had no right to look down on them for expecting hard work. Serving a brother is a reason to work harder. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-timothy-6/
- Ellicott: Slaves must not lean on brotherhood in Christ to treat their masters as equals, since earthly class differences remained. He renders the end of the verse as "those who receive the benefit are believers and beloved." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_timothy/6.htm
- Calvin: The name "brother" might seem to cancel a master's authority, but Paul argues the opposite. Sharing the same adoption by God is an honour that should help slaves serve patiently. https://ccel.org/wwsb/1Timothy/6
- Precept Austin: Disrespect is nothing new. Believers' eternal rewards are linked to how they do their work (Col 3:24–25). https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-timothy-6-commentary

**v. 3**
- Guzik: The danger is the argumentative teacher who drops God's word for his own ideas and treats Scripture as a toy rather than a gift. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-timothy-6/
- Barnes: "Wholesome words" are teachings that keep a church healthy: order, contentment, sober work and patient endurance. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bnb/1-timothy-6.html

**v. 4**
- Calvin: Paul sets "sound" doctrine against this sickly craving for questions. All that clever debate only makes the disease worse. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cal/1-timothy-6.html
- Guzik: Such people rarely call themselves enemies of Scripture. They claim to honour it while twisting it through endless debate to show off. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-timothy-6/
- Precept Austin sets out how NLT, NRSV and RSV word the "morbid craving." https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-timothy-6-commentary

**v. 5**
- Guzik: These teachers' interest in God is partly driven by a desire for wealth and comfort. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-timothy-6/
- GotQuestions: The false teachers are after fame and money. https://www.gotquestions.org/love-money-root-evil.html

**v. 6**
- Guzik: Godliness is great gain only when contentment goes with it. He quotes Barclay that the Greek word *autarkeia* meant self-sufficiency, independent of outward things. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-timothy-6/
- JFB (unabridged): The false teachers are wrong, yet in another sense piety really is great gain. Not the gain they want, but present and eternal gain to the soul. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfu/1-timothy-6.html
- Poole: Godliness cannot be separated from a contented spirit. Another entry on the page says *autarkeia* goes deeper than "contentment": it means being indifferent to whatever one's lot is. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_timothy/6-6.htm
- Barnes: True religion together with peace of mind is the real wealth. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bnb/1-timothy-6.html

**v. 7**
- Guzik: We arrive with nothing and leave with nothing. But we can "send ahead" eternal reward by using our resources well now. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-timothy-6/
- Precept Austin: We didn't even bring ourselves into the world. Compare Job 1:21. https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-timothy-6-commentary

**v. 8**
- Guzik: A contented heart is humble and satisfied with simple things. A culture that over-stimulates us and always wants more works against this. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-timothy-6/
- Precept Austin: Being grateful for the basics guards against covetousness. https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-timothy-6-commentary

**v. 9**
- Guzik: The desire to be rich is more dangerous than riches themselves, and the rich can have it as much as the poor. It is a trap few escape. https://enduringword.com/blog-archive/weekly-devotionals/not-greedy-for-money/
- An entry on biblehub's commentary page: The text speaks of those who *want to be* rich, not those who are rich. Such people give Satan openings, such as dishonest dealing and so much busyness that no time is left for God. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_timothy/6-10.htm

**v. 10**
- GotQuestions: The verse is often misquoted as "money is the root of all evil." Money itself is morally neutral, and sin is the root of evil. https://www.gotquestions.org/love-money-root-evil.html
- Barnes: Taken literally, this can't be true of every evil. It is a popular saying meaning "all sorts of evils." Paul doesn't call money evil. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_timothy/6-10.htm
- Other entries on the same page:
  - Bengel: love of money destroys faith, the root of everything good.
  - Poole: the evil lies in loving money too much.
  - Another entry calls that love idolatry and links it to Judas.
  - Meyer: the "many sorrows" are stings of conscience after leaving the faith.
  - https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_timothy/6-10.htm
- Guzik: Some do leave the faith through greed. Riches don't satisfy. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-timothy-6/

**v. 11**
- Guzik: Timothy must be different from those who live for riches or follow God for what they can get. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-timothy-6/
- JFB: Righteousness concerns other people, and godliness concerns God. Faith is the root of both. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfu/1-timothy-6.html
- Utley at bible.org:
  - The false teachers are not "men of God."
  - *Hupomonē* (perseverance) means enduring hard work and suffering.
  - Timothy must stand firm with a gentle spirit.
  - https://bible.org/seriespage/1-timothy-6

**v. 12**
- JFB: "Fight" (*agōnizou*) picks up the athletic games, perhaps because the letter was written from Corinth (citing Birks). It contrasts with the "strifes of words" in v. 4. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfu/1-timothy-6.html
- Barnes: Grab eternal life the way Greek competitors grabbed the prize. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bnb/1-timothy-6.html
- For what the "good confession" was, see section 2.

**v. 13**
- Utley: God is the source of all life, physical and eternal. https://bible.org/seriespage/1-timothy-6
- JFB: Timothy's encouragement to "take hold of eternal life" rests on the God who keeps his people (1 Pet 1:5). https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfu/1-timothy-6.html
- Entries on biblehub's commentary page:
  - Some say "who gives life" points to God as Preserver more than Creator.
  - Meyer insists the phrase means "before" Pilate, not "in the time of" Pilate. Another entry allows both, and links Christ's confession before the high priest (Mark 14:61–62) with his confession before Pilate that he was King (John 18:37).
  - Bengel: Christ "witnessed" the confession, while Timothy "confessed" it.
  - Geneva note: keep the charge with your eyes on Christ's coming.
  - https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_timothy/6-13.htm
- GotQuestions also points to John 18:37. https://www.gotquestions.org/good-confession.html

**v. 14**
- I found nothing specific beyond the Geneva note above.

**v. 15**
- Calvin: Every earthly government depends on God and rises or falls at his word. Their authority fades, but his lasts forever. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cal/1-timothy-6.html
- Guzik applies the title "King of kings" to Jesus. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-timothy-6/

**v. 16**
- Precept Austin: Only God has immortality in himself, meaning he lasts forever. Nothing else is permanent. https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-timothy-6-commentary

**v. 17**
- Guzik: "In this present age" puts wealth in perspective. The rich must use it responsibly. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-timothy-6/
- Precept Austin: Timothy must keep repeating this charge, because riches warp thinking. Real security is found only in the living God. https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-timothy-6-commentary

**v. 18**
- Precept Austin: The paradox is that we are richer when we give. The rich should invest in the coming age through good works and generosity. https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-timothy-6-commentary

**v. 19**
- JFB: Several ancient manuscripts and the Vulgate read "that which is truly life" rather than "eternal life." https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfu/1-timothy-6.html
- Precept Austin: Wiersbe says the phrase doesn't mean these people are unsaved; it means "the life that is real." It also cites Barnes and the KJV Bible Commentary on "sending treasure ahead." https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-timothy-6-commentary

**v. 20**
- Ellicott: He cites Vincent of Lérins (about AD 430), for whom the "trust" is something received from another, not something you discovered yourself. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_timothy/6.htm
- Precept Austin: The picture is a banker guarding deposits. Wuest says empty chatter becomes filled with evil. https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-timothy-6-commentary

**v. 21**
- Precept Austin:
  - Guthrie: the word for "swerved" is the same one used at the start of the letter.
  - Barclay: don't be too clever to be wise.
  - Demarest: beware of putting your energy into debate instead of faith and love.
  - https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-timothy-6-commentary

## 2. Where interpreters differ (only what I found)

**v. 12, what the "good confession" was.** There are three views.
- **His baptism:**
  - Coffman (Restoration Movement): the "many witnesses" were the church watching the baptism. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-timothy/6-12.html
  - Constable thinks it refers to baptism rather than ordination. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-timothy/6-12.html
  - Gill (Baptist) mentions both his baptism at Lystra and the laying on of hands. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-timothy/6-12.html
- **His ordination:** Stott (Anglican), as reported in the Light of Israel commentary, says "many witnesses" points to ordination. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-timothy/6-12.html
- **A confession under persecution:** Clarke (Methodist) suggests it may have been made when Timothy was imprisoned (Heb 13:23), rather than at his ordination. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-timothy/6-12.html
- Barnes leaves all three options open. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-timothy/6-12.html

**v. 10, "all evil" or "all kinds of evil."** Most commentators read "all kinds," including Barnes (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_timothy/6-10.htm) and GotQuestions (https://www.gotquestions.org/love-money-root-evil.html). John Piper (Baptist) argues the Greek normally means "all evils." In his view, love of money stands for wanting what money buys *instead of* God, so it really is the root of every evil. https://www.desiringgod.org/articles/is-love-of-money-really-the-root-of-all-evils

**vv. 1–2, slavery.** StudyLight shows that 84 commentators split six ways on v. 1, but my copy of the page didn't list the six positions. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-timothy/6-1.html

- Orthodox: oca.org on v. 16 and the "unapproachable light."
